# INTRODUCTION  {#intro}

Marine fishes were once believed to be inexhaustible and immune to the effects of fishing [@mcintoshFisheriesInterNationalCouncil1919a; @nielsenEvolutionFisheriesManagement1976]. However, striking collapses of once-prolific fisheries and delayed or failed recovery  [@hutchingsCollapseRecoveryMarine2000; @frankAlleeEffectsCompensatory2000; @myersMaximumPopulationGrowth1997] have contradicted this perception. The assumption of resilience originated from early theoretical population dynamics modeling [e.g., @verhulstNoticeLoiQue1838] that culminated in the development of modern fisheries science, largely built around the concept of maximum sustainable yield [MSY, @rickerStockRecruitment1954; @schaeferAspectsDynamicsPopulations1954; @bevertonDynamicsExploitedFish1957]. Despite long standing concerns regarding the use of MSY [@finleyAllFishSea2019; @larkinEpitaphConceptMaximum1977], its theoretical underpinning in equilibrium concepts and the associated idea that annual per-capita reproductive output and/or juvenile survival rates increase as abundance declines persisted [@schaeferAspectsDynamicsPopulations1954]. 

Indeed, many modern assessments incorporate a stock-recruit function in which per-capita recruitment increases as biomass declines [@rickerStockRecruitment1954; @bevertonDynamicsExploitedFish1957; @hilbornQuantitativeFisheriesStock1992; @subbeyModellingForecastingStock2014]. Such fisheries assessments implicitly assume that lifetime reproductive rates in the absence of fishing would be expected to be greater than one [@hilbornQuantitativeFisheriesStock1992; @myersPopulationDynamicsExploited1995] and that even heavily-exploited fish stocks retain a innate capacity for recovery [@maceRelationshipsCommonBiological1994]. Although MSY and equilibrium concepts are relatively straightforward, intuitive, and provide a means of developing tractable mechanistic models, questions remain regarding their applicability [@finleyAllFishSea2019; @larkinEpitaphConceptMaximum1977]. There are concerns about whether they accurately reflect the the system being modeled [@hilbornQuantitativeFisheriesStock1992; @paulyPrimaryProductionRequired1995; @wormRebuildingGlobalFisheries2009], particularly for species with markedly different life history characteristics [hilbornFisheriesInducedChangesGrowth2008].  

Life history characteristics (longevity, maximum size, age at maturity) are now considered indicative of a species’ natural mortality, reproductive capacity and overall productivity [@myersStockRecruitmentGeneralizations2001; @roseCompensatoryDensityDependence2001; @winemillerLifeHistoryStrategies2005] and are increasingly used within data-limited assessment approaches to provide management advice [@martellSimpleMethodEstimating2013; @pedersenStochasticSurplusProduction2017] . Ecological theory suggests that 'r-selected' species with small body sizes, characterized by numerous offspring, rapid growth, early maturity and short lifespans, should have greater recovery potential and be better able to withstand fishing pressure [@kindsvaterTenPrinciplesEvolutionary2016; @lawFishingSelectionPhenotypic2000]. Conversely, "K-selected" species with life histories characterized by longer lifespans and later maturity, or those with lower per-capita reproductive output are considered less resilient to fishing pressure and are expected to have a lower recovery potential [@winemillerLifeHistoryStrategies2005].  The life-history traits of 'r-selected' species should manifest in these species having a high innate capacity for population growth in the absence of fishing resulting in these species being able to recovery quickly from low abundance [@essingtonFishingMarineFood2006]. Furthermore, owing to a shared evolutionary history, the life history traits of closely related species are anticipated to be more similar than those of distantly related species [@thorsonPredictingRecruitmentDensity2020]. This implies that there should be less heterogeneity in the productivity among stocks of a single species than between different species with similar life-history traits. However, it remains unclear if correlated and compounding ecological and environmental processes (e.g., climate change effects, predator-prey dynamics) can obscure the importance of life history on realized productivity. This raises concerns that evolutionary history and life history characteristics may serve as a weak foundation for estimating demographic rates for species in which this information is not available. 

Stock assessment data from commercially-harvested marine fishes provide a unique opportunity to explore demographic variability and realized compensatory responses. Focusing on species with a long assessment history means that their life history characteristics are likely to be well-known and that it is possible to quantify realized variability in survival and reproductive output while accounting for the impact of fishery removals. We based our analyses on 77 marine fish stocks from a database of age-specific data [@charbonneauAgestructuredmarinefishdatabase2022]. By constructing life tables (i.e., age-specific estimates of survival and reproduction rates) from abundance-at-age and catch-at-age data, we calculated standard demographic metrics, including  annual population growth rates, doubling time, lifetime reproductive success, and generation time [@caswellMatrixPopulationModels2001]. Our objectives are to 1) Quantify the potential for population growth ($\lambda$) and the strength of density dependence for each stock, 2) quantify recovery potential of each stock, and to 3) explore the variability of these demographic rates regionally and taxonomically. Our results have implications for sustainable management of these commercially-harvested marine fishes and could be used to inform future management actions for stocks that have collapsed.
